quote: The writer should never be ashamed of staring. There is nothing that doesn’t require his attention.
source: Flannery O’Connor, Mystery and Manners, The Nature and Aim of Fiction (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1969)

evidence.where: A course reproduction of the whole essay The Nature and Aim of Fiction downloaded as a PDF and decompressed to text. Both sentences stand verbatim, closing the paragraph on what a teacher can do, immediately after Any discipline can help your writing: logic, mathematics, theology, and of course and particularly drawing. Anything that helps you to see, anything that makes you look. The next paragraph ends The writer's business is to contemplate experience, not to be merged in it. Two secondary citations place that neighbouring sentence on p. 84 of Mystery and Manners, which agrees with the proposal, but no scan of the book itself was opened, so the page number is not claimed in the shipped source and the essay title carries the locator instead. The scanned book at the Internet Archive is lending restricted and its full text could not be searched.
evidence.edition: Mystery and Manners: Occasional Prose, ed. Sally and Robert Fitzgerald, Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1969
evidence.locator: the essay The Nature and Aim of Fiction; p. 84 is probable but not claimed

reason: The wording is exact and the essay attribution is confirmed from the essay's own text, so the line is solid. The only soft part was the page, which rests on secondary citations rather than on a page anyone opened, so it was dropped rather than asserted; the essay title satisfies the locator rule as a named section. O'Connor is not banned, stands at zero for the year, and this line is shipped nowhere. Permission to keep looking is the month's theme and needs no warning.
